utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours and to everyone in the courtroom. Your Honours, that's correct. If Your Honours consider that it's preferable that they be admitted, then, of course, we see no problem with that. And obviously they were in the 92 ter package originally, but it's an attempt of stream-lining while still listing them to be fully clear as to what was used with this witness previously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The Chamber would like to know what your intention is, if you -- because they are all marked for identification. But it is in your hands to decide if you want to tender them -- you have already tendered them, if you want to have them admitted or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would request only for the -- the first indicated exhibits on the current list that we've -- are headed requested to be admitted with the witness now. And for the others, I don't seek admission for them with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Then we should clarify which exhibits exactly you will have tendered, and we will see how to deal with that at the end of the witness's testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: I think that's preferable, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The next witness should be brought in. And for the safety of this witness, the screens should be closed so that the witness can be brought in. The witness has protective measures, especially face distortion and a pseudonym.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. Please stand for a moment and wait so that the screens can be opened. Good afternoon, sir. Would you please read aloud --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Would you please read aloud the affirmation on the card which is shown to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, and now please sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: At the beginning of your evidence, Mr. Elderkin has some questions for you. Mr. Elderkin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness. As you know, my name is --

utterances.speaker: PW-030
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: -- Rupert Elderkin. Before we get started, I just wanted to remind you to try to leave a short pause after your answers so that the interpreters will be able to keep up with us. And if there's anything that I ask to you that's unclear, then please say so and I will do my best to rephrase my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Could I ask, please, for 65 ter 6338 to be brought on screen, and this shouldn't be broadcast. This is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is P513 -- no, sorry, the wrong one.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: For the record, this is Exhibit P543.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Witness, without saying aloud what is written on the screen, please can you confirm if that is your name.

utterances.speaker: PW-030
utterances.text: Yes, that is my name.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd ask for the pseudonym sheet to be admitted under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Witness, do you recall testifying here in December of 2006?

utterances.speaker: PW-030
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Last week did you have a chance to listen to that testimony in your language?

utterances.speaker: PW-030
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Does that testimony fairly, accurately, and truthfully reflect what you would say if you were asked the same questions in court today?

utterances.speaker: PW-030
utterances.text: Yes, I fully agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd move to have the witness's 2006 testimony admitted. And there are both confidential and public versions of that testimony which are marked as P541 and P542, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: They will be received, the first one under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Thank you. And Your Honours' permission, I'd now like to read a short summary of the witness's evidence. And can we start, please, in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: The witness was platoon commander at the southern location. His unit was comprised of two squads, each with a maximum of nine men. In the witness's platoon, everybody had a common interest in doing the job well. As well as taking care of supplies, repairing equipment, making improvements, and carrying out other duties as the leader, the witness also took part in shift duties with the men. The platoon in principle worked six-hour shifts. The southern location was on an elevation with no natural obstacles, allowing for the interception of radio relay communications of the Army of Republika Srpska. The witness's unit received orders from his superiors to monitor particular directions or azimuths, depending on their needs. Every two or three days, it was the witness's duty to review the entire frequency area to see whether there were any new radio relay stations. He would report to his command, and they would decide whether any of them had to be monitored or not. In July of 1995, the witness's unit at the southern location monitored the area of Eastern Bosnia where the Drina Corps was active, and occasionally monitored some other directions. At pages 5031 through 5038 of the witness's Popovic testimony, he described the processes his unit followed in the course of their work. The witness confirmed that he personally transcribed the four intercepts that he was shown and that they were in his handwriting. For one of these intercepts between Popovic and Krstic at 1300 hours on the 2nd of August, 1995, the witness confirmed that his transcription corresponded to an audio recording of the same communication. He explained that his transcription of the communication did not contain the beginning of the conversation heard on the audio recording, as he considered that part was not necessary since it involved Popovic speaking to the operator on duty to establish contact, which the witness did not consider to be significant. Your Honours, that concludes my summary. I have a very few questions which I would like to ask the witness. Could I ask for a packet of intercepts to be handed up to the witness, please. I'd note that there are two yellow stickers I've flagged on pages to which I will refer the witness simply for his convenience. I'd ask first for the witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Sir, please, could you look at the intercept at tab 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And this is 65 ter 3176, and that can be in version B, which should not be broadcast. And this is marked for identification as P527B.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: So I'd simply ask you, looking at this intercept, if you can say on what date this intercept is from?

utterances.speaker: PW-030
utterances.text: Well, I would just like to clarify some things. I'm not sure whether I'm looking at the right page because I have two documents before me, so let me just find my bearings and see which document I should really take a look at. Could you tell me the number of the document? Is that page 03 --

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Excuse me, sir. It's the one you're looking at now. It's the one behind the grey tab number 2.

utterances.speaker: PW-030
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And my question is simply: Can you say what date this intercept is from?

utterances.speaker: PW-030
utterances.text: The date of this communication I don't really see, but I do see the frequency and the time when this conversation took place. I don't see the date of the communication, nor do I see it on the document before this one. In other words, that would mean that the date of this intercept was not really written down, but the time is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And, sir, can you see any date at the top of the report on the page that you're looking at now?

utterances.speaker: PW-030
utterances.text: Yes, I do see that. But before that report, it was crossed out, and I assumed that that wasn't something you were asking me about. But the first one -- yes, the date on the top of the page is the 27th of July, 1995. The 27th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And to confirm, sir, the page you're looking at, is that numbered at the top 0320-4867?

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Could I now ask you to look at the second yellow sticker which is behind the tab number 4 in the packet, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And this is 65 ter number 03214, again the version can be B. And this is P529B, as marked.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, and the date here is from August 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Sir, when reviewing your Popovic testimony last week, did you hear an audio recording of this conversation from August 1995?

utterances.speaker: PW-030
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And can you say why the audio recording for this conversation in particular survived when so many other audio recordings from that time-period were not preserved?

utterances.speaker: PW-030
utterances.text: Well, I cannot tell you exactly why it was preserved, but all the intercepts that we recorded at the location where I was, after the shift changes, some 10 or 15 days, at times the company commander would take them and return them to the command. And that's where they were stored. We did not keep them on site. It was actually done at the command centre. And when our shift was relieved, then our commander would collect all the papers and take them to the command. But why and which intercepts were kept at the command, I really don't know. It was my belief that they would re-listen to all of the intercepts, all of the communications, and hear them again at the command; but why and which ones were kept and whether they were, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Sir, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would ask for the admission of the four intercepts in the packet which were all previously admitted through this witness in the Popovic case, and they are 65 ter numbers 2956A and B, which is marked as P526; and, on the tender list, through P529, which is 65 ter 03214, and that has parts A, B, and C, which is the audio. And the indications as to which parts should be under seal are marked on the tender list. I can read those out if Your Honours wish or leave that just as it is on the list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Just a moment. I would like to check the numbers to avoid any mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Sir -- Your Honour, it's 65 ter number 2956A and B, marked as P526; 65 ter --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It's not necessary to read it out. We have them here on the list, but I just wanted to check the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I am not sure if all of them have a translation. P528A and B don't have a translation yet, so that this one will be marked for identification; the others will be received. Those indicated under seal will be received under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I understand from our Case Manager that there is a translation available for that, so we'll make sure that that makes its way into e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And I have no further questions at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, sir, now the accused, Mr. Tolimir, has the right to put questions to you during his cross-examination. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I bless everybody in and outside of the courtroom, and I wish the court proceedings to end in accordance with God's will and not my own will. I wish to say hello to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to ask the witness to make a pause between question and answer so that the interpreters have enough time to interpret what is being said, as we speak the same language. Thank you. Thank you. Can we show 1D143, please, thank you. In the electronic courtroom. Can we show 1D143 in the e-court. This is his statement. And it should make it easier for him to follow the questions that I'm going to be putting to him. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: These documents shouldn't be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Witness, we see the first page of the statement in Serbian, or in your mother tongue, and in English, and you gave the statement on the 17th and 18th of November, 1999. Did you sign both of these statements?

utterances.speaker: PW-030
utterances.text: My signature is to the right, and that is my signature. I think if I signed that statement I must have signed the other one as well because there is no signature on this other version. But I do remember signing the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I just wanted to ask you if you remember signing the statement in your mother tongue or only in English. Do you remember which one you signed?

utterances.speaker: PW-030
utterances.text: After so many years, I know that I did sign something. I don't know whether I only signed the English version of the statement or the other one because this is not an original document I assume. The one on the right-hand side is. I really cannot remember after so many years which one. I evidently did sign the one in English. That is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Since you did not sign the one in your mother tongue, I'm always going to read to you what you said in the statement. And you're going to tell me whether that is so or not, since I don't know whether you said that and whether you signed it. Because what I'm looking at is actually an unsigned statement. Thank you. Thank you. In paragraph 6 of your statement, line 1, can you please look at that paragraph. This is on page 2. We're going to just take a moment to pull that up. Here it is, paragraph 6 on page 2. You said that you worked at the civilian protection staff. We have that in the first sentence. You said that you worked in the civilian protection staff?

utterances.speaker: PW-030
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I worked in the municipal staff for civilian protection.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Yes. This was until 1993, when you became the platoon commander of the unit for electronic surveillance and communication warfare. Can you please tell us when you moved from the civilian protection staff to the B&H army? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-030
utterances.text: Well, in May 1992, the Executive Board of the Banovici municipality, among other things, members who were in the municipal staff appointed me to that post; and pursuant to the Executive Board of the municipality's decision, I accepted and worked there throughout 1992 and 1993 almost. But since I and my friends and some other people discussed this -- because the work in the municipal staff of civilian protection was something that I didn't like very much because I preferred to work in some kind of communications system. I like that better. So I wanted to move on to some other things. However, during May 1992, I couldn't even suspect how far all these events would go, so I thought that this would be perhaps for a short period of time and then I accept that duty. But this is how my friends and I talked, members of the -- of my radio amateur club, the people that I worked with, who, right from the beginning of the war, were like a communications unit attached to the municipal staff of my municipality. And then sometime in 1993 talks began about how we could help, what exactly we could do. And then there was an idea that came up through some people for us to get in touch with the people in the corps command. We knew what the potential of the southern location was and how much it could do, because with my friends and colleagues I was active from 1979 practically every month to work on radio amateur communications systems at that location. We were allowed to have access to that location --

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: All right. I'm sorry to interrupt. I'm going to put a question to you, and you can fit that into what you're saying.

utterances.speaker: PW-030
utterances.text: That's all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Before you came to this municipal civilian protection staff, before the war, did you also work in that same staff before the war? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-030
utterances.text: No, I didn't work there before the war. I worked on my regular job in a company. I didn't have any contacts there. But what happened was that my colleague in my profession who worked with me was appointed shortly before I was appointed - maybe some 10 or 15 days - as commander of the municipal civilian protection staff. So he got in touch with me first; he thought I could help him in the implementation of some of his plans and jobs in civilian protection regarding the protection of the population and other things. And I did agree. And then on the basis of that, the Assembly -- or rather, the Executive Board of the Assembly, Municipal Assembly, appointed me also as a member of the staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And you were in the southern location; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PW-030
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In paragraph 6 of your statement that we saw right now on the screen and quoted in the last sentence, it says that you were demobilised on the 15th of March, 1996; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PW-030
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. That is what the certificate says.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question would be: Since you worked both in the southern and the northern locations, what was the difference between the northern and the southern location as far as the equipment that you used, the apparatus that you used? Is there a major difference? Or if there isn't, you could just say that there isn't any difference. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-030
utterances.text: There was no major difference. The equipment was similar or the same. But the southern location provided greater capabilities for eavesdropping because of its elevation of some 300 metres above sea level. So it provided better work conditions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please tell us whether it ever happened that the same document was recorded, the same conversation was recorded, both on the southern and on the northern location. And if this did happen, can you please tell us how this is possible. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-030
utterances.text: Well, you see that from the technical aspect it's a realistic possibility. Not only did the same conversations get recorded at both locations, but there was another unit other than my unit at the northern facility which was doing some other things. And sometimes it would happen that all of us would record the same conversation and then everybody would dispatch that transcribed conversation to wherever they were supposed to send that. And I don't know what happened after that, where these conversations were passed on to, but this would happen frequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you please tell us, Could you record the same participants in the same radio network from the beginning of the conversation to the end, could you note down their names; and was this recorded at the same time, or was there any time difference when these conversations were recorded?

utterances.speaker: PW-030
utterances.text: There was no time difference. It was all done simultaneously. There was no delay. If something was being done, then it was being done 100 per cent at the same time. Perhaps there could be a couple of minutes' difference in the report because somebody's clock was not showing exactly the same time. These were units that had different authorisations, different contacts. They didn't contact each other at the northern location as far as their work was concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. Please can you tell us if it's possible for a conversation of two participants in the same network to be recorded at the same time by the northern and the southern location, and would the time of them have to be the same if they had both been recorded right from the beginning? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-030
utterances.text: Well, I said that this was possible if the clocks were synchronised. If they were not, if the clocks were showing different times by a few minutes, then they would not be recorded as having been recorded at the same time. But the conversation actually did take place at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: If there was no time difference, it means that they were recorded simultaneously?

utterances.speaker: PW-030
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. But between the northern and the southern location, what could have happened was, because their positions and their azimuths was not the same, you could have the case where a conversation recorded at the southern facility would not be able to hear one speaker and at the northern location you could hear both participants, or you couldn't hear the one that the other location could hear because the angles of recording were different. So this is something that can happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, Mr. Tolimir, I had to stop you. May I remind both speakers to slow down a little bit and not to overlap. It is very difficult for the interpreters. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I said the same participants in the same radio network and that everything was recorded at the same time, the frequency, the time, the names, this is what I emphasise. And thank you. And, now, can you please tell me, can you answer the following question: Is it possible -- actually, how long did the conversations that you recorded and that you have in this notebook here, how long did they last?

utterances.speaker: PW-030
utterances.text: Conversations would last for a couple of minutes or so. I never timed them. But these were not long conversations.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Would a conversation last for five minutes?

utterances.speaker: PW-030
utterances.text: I never really thought about it. Possibly, possibly not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Look, look, can you please look at these conversations that are in front of you and tell me whether any of them took longer than five minutes?

utterances.speaker: PW-030
utterances.text: Well, the first one didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-030
utterances.text: And let's look at this other one, yeah, that didn't last longer than five minutes either. Yeah, these two conversations that I have here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. So, in any case, no conversation took longer than five minutes. Were there any cases in your experiences, in your practice, that a conversation took longer than five minutes, and were these official conversations - thank you - that you recorded?

utterances.speaker: PW-030
utterances.text: I did record conversations that were sometimes an hour long, but I don't remember whether I ever actually transcribed any of those conversations from the tape. Because of other duties, I usually didn't have time to do that. So I would ask one of my younger soldiers who was free to transcribe that conversation. But these were conversations that were conducted by Mr. Karadzic, Biljana Plavsic, Krajisnik, Koljevic, when they talked about their correspondence in London, in Moscow, Paris, who gave them different kinds of advice and tricks to apply, including the arrest and the tying up of those UNPROFOR soldiers. These were suggestions that they received from abroad and which I heard. And I recorded some of those conversations. But I don't remember transcribing such a long conversation ever. I don't think that I ever did, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: On page 3 --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at page 3 of the witness's statement, paragraph 3 on page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You can see it, and you said: "When an operator heard a voice, he would stop the scanner and turn it to the appropriate channel." Did you say that? Did you state that? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-030
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. My question is: How long did you need to stop the scanner, adjust the channel, and begin the recording of the conversation? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-030
utterances.text: In order to stop the channel, you needed less than a second; and then in the second second, you could -- or second or two, you could go back those two or three channels and then the conversation would be recorded. When the scanning stopped, you needed two seconds at the most to activate the button on the tape recorder and to begin taping the conversations. So it was a very short amount of time. From the moment we heard the conversation, we could begin recording it within a second or two.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you explain to us, would you lose anything of the conversation that was important? And on the basis of the rest of the conversation, could you figure out what was being talked about in that one second? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-030
utterances.text: Well, look at this. It's evident that there is a large number of conversations where it is clearly stated that the recording was not -- that the conversation was not recorded from the beginning. What does that mean? There were 24 channels at the radio relay system; they were scanned within a few seconds. We would adjust the speed, whether this would take 3, 5, or 7 seconds to scan. And then what could happen simply is that we would not hear the beginning of a conversation for a number of reasons. One of the reasons was that we were not near that channel, so it was necessary to get there. Also, once we got to the channel, perhaps the participants at that moment were not speaking. So it was quiet for a second or two, so we wouldn't hear anything. But if something was heard, a change of tone in the signal, then it would be enough just to push the button on the tape recorder and the recording would begin -- actually, the receiver button, not the tape recorder button. Then the scanning would stop, we would go back one or two channels that we had skipped, and we would come to the conversation, and we would immediately or simultaneously, at the same time, begin recording. And that's why we have conversations that were not recorded from the beginning. What we didn't hear from the beginning, we would simply say, The conversation was not recorded from the beginning. And then we heard and began, we would start writing it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I understood you. So we just heard from you that the scanning takes about a second before you can actually press the necessary buttons. Now, please tell us, what happens - as you described in paragraph 4, in lines 1, 2, and 3 - where you said: "Sometimes after the operator recorded a conversation and turned the scanner back on, he would hear the middle of another conversation on a different channel. When this happened, he would immediately begin recording it, but the first part of that conversation would be lost." Just a moment, please, for the transcript.

utterances.speaker: PW-030
utterances.text: Yes, I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, could you please explain, What did you do in case where you had a conversation that had been lost or where you had the conversation that you started monitoring at halfway?

utterances.speaker: PW-030
utterances.text: Well, what we mean here by "lost," means that it was lost. We did not discuss it nor did we think about it. We did not record it, so it wasn't ever presented as having taken place. We would just say that the conversation was not recorded from the start and that it was recorded from the moment where it started and then onward. And then we would transcribe that into a notebook. Then it would be typed into a computer, where the computer would send it to another computer, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. But my question was: Would you preserve the portion of the conversation that you managed to actually monitor?

utterances.speaker: PW-030
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The accused did not turn on his microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And on page 37, that's one paragraph before last in your statement, where you say that there were some other people with you at the southern location - you mentioned their names here; I won't read them out because I don't want us to go into closed session - but could you please tell us what did these people do? Because you said in your statement that they did similar work to yours.

utterances.speaker: PW-030
utterances.text: Well, where I said that it was similar work, in signals communication and in the Yugoslav Army this was a broad field. These people actually dealt in signals work, so they actually monitored; they did surveillance. They were on a high elevation, and they transmitted and maintained communications within the BH Army. Their job was different. They had their own work to do. They had different facilities. And I never asked about their work. And as a person who was well acquainted with the communications work, I did -- I knew what they were doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. So they actually recorded radio communications?

utterances.speaker: PW-030
utterances.text: No, no, they did not. They would just maintain the networks. There was the -- these digiputer communications where they would communicate between two different computers at two different elevations, and they would then forward those communications on and so on. So that was the kind of work they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. But could you tell us now whether you yourself actually listened in on conversations within the BH Army?

utterances.speaker: PW-030
utterances.text: No, we never engaged in that kind of work. We did not monitor the communications within the BH Army, but we did monitor the communications in the Serbian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, is it normal and regular practice, standard practice, in all armies in the world, that signals units would actually control the work of the -- and the communications that were transmitted within their own ranks and not only those that were transmitted in the enemy ranks?

utterances.speaker: PW-030
utterances.text: Well, you see, my task was only to monitor the communications of the Republika Srpska Army. It is possible that there was someone else who would do the same kind of work. But monitoring the communications within the BH Army, I don't know about that. I don't know anything about that. But, personally, I was never involved in that kind of work nor was it my job. And I did not really take this seriously as being a military type operation, although when I was in the Yugoslav Army I was pretty well informed of how the system worked within an organised army. But this was a different type of operation, a different scale and scope, and we just did the work as we did it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now show the witness page 4 of his statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And, Witness, would you please look at the first paragraph because I would like to put a question to you about what you said there. You say in the third sentence of the first paragraph on page 4 -- can you see that? Can you see the third sentence, the third line?

utterances.speaker: PW-030
utterances.text: Is that in the first paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Yes. The third sentence in the first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: PW-030
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In English that will be on an earlier page. You say here in the third sentence: "At the end of each shift, the company commander of the 2nd Corps," captain so and so, "would usually come to pick us up, and he would bring with him the relief shift. Then we would hand-over all the notebooks that we had and the tapes. Before we left the facility, we would have a meeting in order to convey all the relevant information to the new squad." My question is: If this is correct, if this is what you said, then I would -- first of all, I would like to ask you: Is it -- was this correctly recorded? Is this what you said?

utterances.speaker: PW-030
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Well, then my question is this: When did you begin to receive these notebooks that the commander would then take to the corps command at the end of the shift? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-030
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't really tell you when exactly this practice began. At first we just transcribed all these conversations on bits of paper which we would then burn; but then someone from the command - I don't know if it was the company commander or someone else -- sometime in 1994 I believe, I can't recall exactly at what time, these notebooks appeared. And at first we didn't quite understand what they were for. At the time I couldn't even imagine that some day they would be used the way they're used here today. Because up until then we had destroyed a lot of such materials and -- up until 1994. But then when these notebooks appeared, then we began writing everything down in the notebooks and that that was what was preserved.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, could you tell us whether these notebooks were certified in any way, and why was it that you had to return them, and were you issued these notebooks? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-030
utterances.text: I cannot remember whether I had to sign any receipt or anything for these notebooks because the practice was that when the next shift arrived all the tapes that had been recorded by the previous shift or that they had taken to the centre for re-listening and deleting if necessary -- so it was normal for those notebooks, too, to be sent together with the tapes, primarily because I was pretty certain that somebody would listen to the tapes again. There were people at the command who would do this work at the command. They would analyse all the recorded intercepts, and then they would figure out the units, their areas of responsibility, their areas of operation, the names of the individuals in charge of those units, what locations they were at, and so on; because this would help you then draw up or get a picture of the Republika Srpska Army and their command structure and system. So to me, this seemed so normal that I didn't really pay any particular attention to it because I had no idea that some day they would be used for anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us now whether all these four intercepts in notebook 22 that you mention in paragraph 4 of your statement, whether these are those four intercepts? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-030
utterances.text: Do you mean the four intercepts that I actually -- the four conversations that I recorded?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PW-030
utterances.text: Well, yes. These were the conversations that I recorded myself, transcribed them, and then I signed them; although there were numerous intercepts that I made, but I did not transcribe them. And then I did not sign off on that. Somebody else would have had to do it in my place.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please take a look at paragraph 5 of your statement where you say that you recorded these conversations at the frequency 255.80 [as interpreted], and you say that at around 10.00 you recorded these two conversations. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: PW-030
utterances.text: No, I can't find that. I can't see that, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: It says 10 -- at 1000, 1000 hours, that's what it says in the first line. Can you find that? Can you see it? Can you see 1000 hours in the first line of paragraph 5? "I was asked to look at a conversation in notebook 22, page 12, timed at 1000 hours ..." You can see it on the monitors -- on the monitor before you. Is that what you stated?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: That's paragraph 5 on page 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Before this -- before these numbers, 1 and 2, can you see: "I was asked to look at a conversation in notebook 22, page 12, timed at 1000 hours ..." Can you see it?

utterances.speaker: PW-030
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So my question for you is: Who was it that asked you to look at this conversation and when?

utterances.speaker: PW-030
utterances.text: Well, this was during the proofing session. I think when I first came to The Hague to testify, this must have been at least ten years ago. I think this was in 2001 or so, so I can't really tell you who it was who asked me, but it was here on the premises of the Tribunal during a proofing session where I was asked what I recorded, what I transcribed, and so on. And about this one, I said that I wasn't the one who recorded that conversation but that I was present while there and that it was done by somebody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So this wasn't a conversation that you actually intercepted and recorded; correct?

utterances.speaker: PW-030
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it possible that somebody at the northern location recorded this same conversation at the same time, at the same frequency, 255.850?

utterances.speaker: PW-030
utterances.text: Not only was there a person at the northern location, but it was actually recorded there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Well, is it possible that it was recorded at the northern location five minutes later?

utterances.speaker: PW-030
utterances.text: No way, unless the clocks were not synchronised, there was some error with the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you see the last sentence here? You say at the last -- in the last sentence on page 4 you say: "On November 17th, 1999, I provided a sample of my handwriting and did not have access to any notebook while doing so." Is this something that you stated?

utterances.speaker: PW-030
utterances.text: Well, obviously if that's how it's recorded then that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, my question is: Who was it who took a sample of your handwriting and why was it done and did you ever find out what the outcome was?

utterances.speaker: PW-030
utterances.text: Well, you see, in November 1999 when I gave my statement - because I don't know who else might have given a statement and given their samples of handwritings, but I can speak for myself -- I won't mention the names of any other people for different reasons, but I know who they were, and, if necessary, I can tell you their names. But these were people who came to check what knowledge we had, what kind of experience we had, and what kind of work we had done. And, of course, I did give my sample -- a sample of my handwriting because I'm sure that if someone found notes that I wrote, they would be able to actually recognise my handwriting. So I only provided a sample. I don't know how many words or sentences I wrote down. So I only gave a sample so that they could compare it with a text that they had.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Where did -- where was it that you gave this sample of your handwriting? Here at the Tribunal or ...

utterances.speaker: PW-030
utterances.text: No, this was at my place of residence. It was a one-time National Defence Secretariat office building; that was what it used to be. Where it was at the time when I provided my -- the sample of my handwriting, I don't recall anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Were there any representatives of The Hague Tribunal on the premises while you were giving a sample of your handwriting?

utterances.speaker: PW-030
utterances.text: I don't know whether it was just my understanding, but I believe -- I believed so because knowing the persons that I met with later on I think that was the case. But I'm not sure whether both those people were there because I didn't see this other individual, this other person was an interpreter. But I can't tell you precisely whether she was or wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. So was this sample of your handwriting taken from you by the person who conducted this interview with you?

utterances.speaker: PW-030
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell us, please, speaking of notebooks and handwriting, you mention notebook 22, which I just mentioned a moment ago. Was there a cover page; do you recall? And what did it look like?

utterances.speaker: PW-030
utterances.text: Well, you see, when we first received these notebooks, they did not look very serious. They were funny. These were notebooks for elementary school students. There were some pictures on their covers, and they were coloured. And this was unusual for the type of work that we did, which was serious. But these were notebooks that were probably provided by some humanitarian organisation for -- as aid for schools and school children, and that's how we got a number of such notebooks.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And can you please tell us what was written on that notebook, number 22, that you got?

utterances.speaker: PW-030
utterances.text: That was -- it just had the number on it, because the notebooks were numbered.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Were there any drawings or pictures on it?

utterances.speaker: PW-030
utterances.text: They all had pictures or different drawings. I don't exactly remember what was on notebook number 22. I didn't really analyse the drawings.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. We're coming back, now, to paragraph number 1 on page 4 of this statement of yours where you say that -- in the third sentence -- actually, in the one sentence but last -- actually, in the last sentence you say: "Before leaving the site, a briefing would be held to make the incoming squad aware of relevant information." Did you say that? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-030
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question is: Who would give the briefing, and what were the contents of the briefing? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-030
utterances.text: The briefing would be given by the commander of the company. I was there as the platoon commander. Also, the commanders of the squads were there because they replaced each other, and the squads were from two different locations, two different towns. We didn't really have contacts. So then when we were handing over the shift, it was customary to inform them about the problems; the dynamics; what was happening in our shift; the directions that needed to be monitored, depending on where the combat actions were taking place at that particular time. The incoming shift had to be informed about all the issues relating to the previous shift.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you please tell me if you informed the soldiers about the situation at the front in the area of responsibility of the units that they were listening in on? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-030
utterances.text: I don't know which soldiers you mean. Are you thinking of my soldiers specifically or some others?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I'm thinking of those that you would brief before leaving your shift. Would you inform them what the situation was on the front among those that you were listening in on?

utterances.speaker: PW-030
utterances.text: Sometimes it was necessary to, for example, give information in the event of the Olovo front where the situation was very tense. When the shifts switched, we would warn the next shift so that it would approach their assignments with greater responsibility and seriousness in order to be able to carry out their assignment successfully. We would expect the next shift to treat their assignments with the same seriousness and professionalism that we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Since this was a complex situation and it was necessary to monitor a number of columns, the breakthrough of the units, the situation among the population, would you inform them of those matters as well, and what did you tell them if you were informing them about this kind of situation as well?

utterances.speaker: PW-030
utterances.text: Since we were listening in on the main axes, which included the main Serbian forces and the General Staff, we would pass on the information that they exchanged amongst themselves about certain activities and affairs. This is what we would pass on. We didn't know what was going on in some units, however. And ultimately this was not something that we recorded and that was not something that we could talk about. I myself personally at the beginning had no idea until these events came to light later exactly what was going on, and I found out about a lot of things only later. At the time when the activities were actually ongoing, we didn't write down and we didn't know what was going on in the other units. I don't have any other information and didn't have any information about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Since you've been a radio amateur for a long time and you've been working on communications and things like that, did you ever attend any training or courses on these topics?

utterances.speaker: PW-030
utterances.text: I've attended lots of courses. For at least 20 years I was recruited by the chief or communications commander of the then-5th Army District. They wanted me to join the army and become active. I never liked the army, never accepted that, and I don't regret not joining to this very day. I attended many courses, including those for encryption and deciphering of encryption, other than courses that had to do with actual communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Other than courses in the JNA, did you attend any courses in any other organisations?

utterances.speaker: PW-030
utterances.text: No. I never attended any other courses outside of those in the JNA on these particular matters, but I learned a lot about ham radio operators, the types of communications, things like that. If I were to tell somebody about all the types of communications that ham radio operators use, they probably wouldn't believe me to this very day.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you ever travel abroad during the war? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-030
utterances.text: No, I didn't, not during the war. Up until the war and after the war, I did; but during the war, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. Thank you for your specific and professional answers. Thank you for the conversation that we had. I wish you a safe journey and return home, and may God bless you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have completed my cross-examination of this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Tolimir. Mr. Elderkin, do you have re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: No, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: At this stage, I would like to ask you, Mr. Elderkin, do you wish to withdraw materials previously tendered and marked for identification for this witness? I think we have to talk about P530 through P540 and P544 through P547. These are on your exhibit list, but not admitted today. What is your intention?

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm just following that on the marked tendered list. So I understand, obviously, that the previously admitted exhibits, which I see all bear the 200 series numbers, are already in. I would withdraw the ones that you just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, are there any objections from the Defence to the Prosecution withdrawing these materials?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We don't have any objection. The only thing is that we would like it always to be like that. When a document is being tendered, we would like to know more about it because the number doesn't really say anything about the contents. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Elderkin and myself, we were referring to the list of documents tendered by the Prosecution through this witness, a list prepared by the Registry yesterday. The Chamber, therefore, orders that the exhibits identified by the Prosecution as having been withdrawn from the record have their status changed to "marked but not admitted." In future, the Chamber expects the Prosecution to clearly indicate on the record and in a timely manner if it decides to withdraw any materials previously offered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Understood. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Some other matters I just received from Madam Registrar: The information that the document P528A and B in fact have a translation, so that they will be received as well. Mr. Tolimir, you used the OTP statement with this witness. Are you tendering it?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I don't wish to tender the statement. The witness acknowledged that he had said everything that is written in the statement. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sir, this concludes the examination. You are now free to return to your normal activities and to your place of residence. Thank you very much for your attendance here. And the Chamber wants to express its gratitude and all the best for your future. Thank you very much again. I think it could be a convenient time to have the first break now so that the witness can be -- can leave the courtroom protected. We should have the first break now and resume ten minutes -- no, five minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could the next witness be brought in. Mr. Elderkin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Your Honours, while we're waiting for the next witness, I wanted to raise one point which I think might just be a very minor housekeeping. There is one of the intercepts which is taken down by this witness in his handwriting, in fact, has already been admitted. It's P278A. And it's described in e-court as being an intercept dated the 14th of July, 1995, 11.49 hours, handwritten from notebook 84. I've checked, and it's actually an intercept from notebook 1, Your Honours. I wanted to state that on the record, and I'm not sure what process we need to follow if we want to change the description in e-court. But it's simply a matter for record that I showed the accused's legal advisor this afternoon. I think it's agreed that that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could you please indicate the 65 ter number in your exhibit list, then we can identify the document better.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: It's 65 ter 2978A, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. Would you please read aloud the affirmation on the card which is shown to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And, now, please sit down. Mr. Elderkin, your correction you have made in the list of documents, it's now on the record, and I think it's correct that you are referring to notebook number 1. Thank you. Mr. Elderkin, you may proceed with the witness. Please be reminded, as Mr. Tolimir as well, that you switch off the microphone while the witness is speaking. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness. As you know, my name is Rupert Elderkin. And before we get started, I'd ask for you to make sure that you leave a pause after your answers so that the interpreters have time to keep up with us. And also, as you have the protective measure of voice protection, as the President has mentioned, please don't speak while you see the red light at the top of my microphone. And I'll switch it off when I've finished asking my questions. If I ask you anything that's unclear to you, then please say so and I'll do my best to rephrase my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Could I start, first of all, by asking for 65 ter 6298, which is marked as P558, to be shown. And it should not be broadcast, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Sir, without saying aloud what is written on the screen, can you please confirm if that is your name?

utterances.speaker: PW-042
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: I'd ask, Your Honours, for that to be admitted under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Sir, do you recall testifying here in January 2007?

utterances.speaker: PW-042
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And did you have a chance to listen to that testimony in your language yesterday?

utterances.speaker: PW-042
utterances.text: Yes, I listened to my entire testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Does that testimony fairly, accurately, and truthfully reflect what you would say if you were asked the same questions in court today?

utterances.speaker: PW-042
utterances.text: Well, it wouldn't be identical probably, but the context of all the answers would be the same, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd move now to have the witness's 2007 testimony admitted. It's 65 ter 6299, which is marked as P556 and is under seal; and the public version is 65 ter 6300, marked as P557.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Both will be received, the first under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, is there any problem with the monitor? We can pause a short moment. I think the problem will be solved. Thank you. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And again, with permission, Your Honours, I'd like to read a very brief summary of the witness's evidence, which is based on his Popovic testimony and also on the underlying witness statement used for that testimony. If we could start in private session, please, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: The witness completed his mandatory --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're now in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: One month later, he was transferred to the ABiH 2nd Corps' electronic reconnaissance and anti-electronic activities unit, based at the northern location. He remained in this post until he left the army in 1997. The witness was on duty as an intercept operator at the northern location in July of 1995. At the time, he was able to identify individual voices, including Zivanovic, Krstic, Pantic, and Legenda. He identified seven intercepts from July 1995 as being in his handwriting, and he confirmed that he transcribed them on the dates that they were intercepted. I have a few further questions, with Your Honours' permission. And I'd ask for the usher to hand the witness a file containing some intercepts.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Sir, yesterday did you have a chance to review this file?

utterances.speaker: PW-042
utterances.text: I've reviewed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And the file contains both handwritten and printed versions of 12 intercepted conversations; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PW-042
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Did you also see the original handwritten notebooks containing the 12 intercepts?

utterances.speaker: PW-042
utterances.text: I did see the original notebook.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And did the intercepts in the blue file you have in front of you correspond with the original notebooks?

utterances.speaker: PW-042
utterances.text: They are identical in terms of content, so the intercepts in the notebook and the ones that are typed out are identical.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Can you confirm that all 12 intercepts in the file are in your handwriting?

utterances.speaker: PW-042
utterances.text: All the 12 intercepts are in my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Did you intercept and transcribe all 12 conversations?

utterances.speaker: PW-042
utterances.text: I intercepted all 12 of them and transcribed them into notebooks.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And for each of those 12 intercepts, did you have a chance yesterday also to see the print-out versions of the intercepts in the file?

utterances.speaker: PW-042
utterances.text: I also saw the printed-out version.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Do the printed versions correspond to the handwritten intercepts?

utterances.speaker: PW-042
utterances.text: They do correspond; they're identical, the printed version and the handwritten version.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Sir, generally, when you were working as an intercept operator, how soon after intercepting a conversation did you transcribe it into a notebook?

utterances.speaker: PW-042
utterances.text: Well, we did not transcribe every conversation. Depending on how clear the recording is and how clear the voice is -- in other words, those conversations that were clearer, that could be heard more clearly, they would be transcribed more quickly into notebooks; whereas with those conversations where you couldn't understand some parts, we had to repeat them and re-listen to them several times in order to verify the understanding and what we had written down in the notebooks.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: But would the transcription nevertheless take place on or about the day on which the conversation was intercepted?

utterances.speaker: PW-042
utterances.text: The intercepts were transcribed immediately, as soon as the conversation between the participants ended. So the conversations would be transcribed as soon as the conversation ended, and they would be transcribed in notebooks.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would, at this point, request the admission of all 12 of these intercepts. Seven of the intercepts were previously admitted through the witness in the Popovic case, and they are on the tender list marked as P549 through P555. And the five intercepts which were not previously admitted through this witness are P559 through P563, and the tender list indicates which versions should be under seal. And, in addition, I would request the admission of the witness's May 1999 statement which was the underlying statement of his evidence used in the Popovic case and admitted in that case, and that's marked as P548, under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And which intercepts are contained in the file we have received in hard copy?

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Your Honours, all 12 intercepts are in the file. The first seven tabs in the file contain the seven previously admitted intercepts, and the five additional intercepts are at tabs 8 through 12.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. They will be received. And I think they all have a translation so that they will be received, some of them under seal as indicated on the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours. And I have no further questions for the witness at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Sir, now the accused has the right to put questions to you. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And good afternoon, Witness. I hope you have a pleasant stay here. And I would like to say to you, as Mr. Elderkin did, that we need to make pauses between questions and answers in order for the transcript to be properly recorded. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now please show in e-court the statement of this witness. The number is 0087-5367 -- or rather, this document: P584 [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we show the first page of the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... to interrupt. P548. P548, because it was recorded as P584. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P584. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Once again, you are referring to which OTP statement?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I see it already in e-court. Could we just also see the version in the native tongue of this witness so that he can follow my questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is Exhibit P548.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I apologise to the Presiding Judge. You were correct. It is P548. I apologise. I mixed up the numbers. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Witness, what you can see on the monitor is -- on the left-hand side, you can see your statement in your mother tongue; and on the right-hand side, it's the English translation. This is your statement provided on the 7th and the 11th of May, 1999. Tell us, please, did you sign these statements? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-042
utterances.text: The signature and -- on the English version is mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And did you also sign your statement in your mother tongue? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-042
utterances.text: I cannot really recall. I can't tell you whether I did or didn't sign it in the mother tongue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. As you cannot say it for certain, I will quote portions of your statement. And then what you need to do is just confirm that you've actually said that or not. Thank you. Did you understand me?

utterances.speaker: PW-042
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now please see page 2 of this statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And, Witness, would you please take a look at paragraph 3. We can see it already before us. Tell me, please, were you employed at the Secretariat for National Defence in the place as stated in the statement? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-042
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you work there until 1988? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-042
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. What did you do as of 1988? And if you were employed, were you still employed within some military structures or armed forces? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-042
utterances.text: I was not employed with the military. I worked in a company as a ONO/DSZ desk officer, and you know what that referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you receive your salary from the federal organs? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-042
utterances.text: Which period are you referring to when you're asking me about my salary?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, while you were at the Secretariat for National Defence and at the time when you were a desk officer of DSZ/ONO. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-042
utterances.text: While I was employed at the Secretariat for National Defence, we were actually funded by the municipal authorities. And, after that, I received my pay from the company where I was employed, not from any state or government organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. We have to explain for the transcript that ONO/DSZ refers to All People's Defence and Social Self Protection. This is for transcript purposes. Thank you. Thank you. Now, in paragraph 4 you mentioned that you were employed with the Territorial Defence. This is in the first line of your -- of paragraph 4 of your statement? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-042
utterances.text: Well, when the war started in May 1992, the Territorial Defence was established, and all citizens joined the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did the BH Army take over all the Territorial Defence units, as you state here? And this was also the manner in which your brigade was formed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-042
utterances.text: Well, after I was expelled from my hometown when I came to another town, they already had a brigade that had been established earlier, so we were just attached to that local brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I was asking you about the brigades. Did this -- was this brigade actually built on the one-time TO defence?

utterances.speaker: PW-042
utterances.text: Well, the -- I joined the 107th Brigade in November 1992 at the time when it had already been established. Now, as for what it had been earlier, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. When Mr. Elderkin asked you about this a little earlier, that's what you confirmed. Thank you. Please tell us, When did you start working as an intercept operator and at what facilities?

utterances.speaker: PW-042
utterances.text: Since 19 -- as of 1993, I was at the northern location.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please take a look at paragraph 9 of your statement, starting with the word "our task," as you can see here. That's the one paragraph before last, one full paragraph before last. And in the last sentence of that paragraph, you say: "In order to do this, I would be expected to listen in on radio communications for between three and eight hours, depending on how busy we were. I would then have a period of rest." Have I read out your statement correctly?

utterances.speaker: PW-042
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. My question then is: Does this mean that you worked on average five hours when you are referring to this time-period? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-042
utterances.text: Well, the time-frame was eight hours per shift. Now, how much work we had at -- in that shift, that depended on the situation and the radio communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. But here in this paragraph you say that you worked between 3.00 and 8.00 p.m. Does that mean that you spent five hours listening-in on radio communications? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-042
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us, please, whether five hours of monitoring networks and participants in radio communications would be a very tiring exercise for an operator?

utterances.speaker: PW-042
utterances.text: Well, that would depend on how busy the traffic was. It wasn't that we had the same number of intercepts every day. Depending on how busy the radio communications were would also -- we would be engaged for that number of hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. But if it was a busy day, would that affect the quality and the hearing of the operators; or would the operators, because they would get tired, actually become less efficient? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-042
utterances.text: Well, if we felt that we were tired or were not focused enough and weren't able to do our job properly, then we would ask our colleagues who were supposed to come and relieve us to come earlier. So the following shift would then be asked to come earlier in order to relieve us.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you please take a look at paragraph 10 of your statement, the penultimate sentence, that's the second sentence, you say - that's on page 2, paragraph 10 of your statement - and you say the following: "The commander would also give a briefing on occasions. "The commander would also give a briefing on occasions." Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: PW-042
utterances.text: Yes, I've seen it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you please tell us, What kind of briefings were these and what type of instructions did the commander issue and what did they relate to? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-042
utterances.text: The commander who was with us in the shift was responsible for the axes, the frequencies that we were supposed to monitor at any given time. If the commander was privy to some information that we needed to change -- to alter some frequencies, he would come to the office where we were working and would adjust the frequencies, and then we would monitor those frequencies, whereas the frequencies that we had monitored earlier would now be unmonitored.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown page 3 of the statement in B/C/S and the corresponding page in English in order for the witness to be able to follow my questions. Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Please take a look at paragraph 1, lines 6 and 7 in that paragraph. You say the following: "Transcribing sometimes involved listening in on a conversation or parts of a conversation several times." My question is this: Sir, please tell us, What was the audibility at the site where you had to listen to a conversation on several occasions? What -- how was -- was it intelligible, what you heard, or was there jamming?

utterances.speaker: PW-042
utterances.text: Well, transcribing the conversations -- or the intercepts, actually, depended on -- not only on how well we could hear the conversations but also depending on the participants. Because sometimes there would be noises in the channel because these were communications transmitted by air, and sometimes we had to listen to the same conversation on several -- several times over in order to make sure that the words that were said in the conversations were understood properly and properly transcribed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. So this monitoring or listening to the conversations only related to the intelligibility of what was being listened to; correct? Just answer yes or no.

utterances.speaker: PW-042
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Please tell me, if you were unable to understand something, would you then fill in the gaps, judging what it should read like, judging by the context?

utterances.speaker: PW-042
utterances.text: If I wasn't certain, while transcribing an intercept, I would ask my colleagues to help me in order to transcribe the intercepted conversations as correctly as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please now take a look at paragraph 4, it consists of one sentence only, and relates to all the completed notebooks. It says: "Completed notebooks ..." Those are the first words in paragraph 4 on page 3. You say that they would be placed in an archive. Could you describe this procedure. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-042
utterances.text: All the notebooks that we filled in at the location where we worked when the shifts were changed were taken to the command, where they would archive them, because filled notebooks did not stay at the location where we were.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And can you please tell us, When this practice was introduced, when was it introduced as compared to the length of time that you worked at that location where you worked? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-042
utterances.text: When I came to the northern location, it was immediately the practice that all the completed notebooks on the change-over of the shifts would be taken to the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know why they were kept there, and were there any exceptions, for example, that somebody would keep a notebook with them? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-042
utterances.text: The notebooks were not kept at the location, the ones that we used to transcribe the conversations. As for what happened at the command, I really don't know anything about that, so I wouldn't be able to tell you what happened with the notebooks.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you please look at paragraph 4 of your statement where you say: "I have been asked if the same message was ever recorded and transcribed twice. I can confirm that this did happen occasionally, usually when the same conversations were monitored on different frequencies by different sites." My question to you is: Could you please explain what you meant by this sentence, and when did this happen? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-042
utterances.text: The communications systems themselves had a number of transmissions systems, a number of transmitters, and they reached specific locations along a specific channel or frequency, and then they were rerouted along a different channel and frequency. So what is written here actually relates to the actual transmission technology used to transmit information.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. When you say "another location," do you mean the northern or the southern location, or some other location that happened to be in the north or the south? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-042
